precepts.text: Your lamb shall be without blemish; it was taken out from the sheep, kept from the goats to the fourteenth day, and roasted with fire, not raw nor sodden.
precepts.point: The Passover lamb shows how that was carried out. The lamb was without blemish, a male of the first year, taken out from the sheep and kept from the goats, because if it got in a fight it would take a blemish, a bruise, a cut. It was kept up to the fourteenth day, isolated and given nothing but water, so that it purified itself; and it was eaten roast with fire, not raw and not sodden with water, with the purtenance thereof, for after those days there was nothing left within it.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
The Passover lamb shows how offering without blemish was carried out. “Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year: ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats”. It was taken out from the sheep and kept from the goats, because if it got in a fight it would take a blemish, a bruise, a cut.

Then “ye shall keep it up until the fourteenth day of the same month”: from the tenth day to the fourteenth it was isolated and given nothing but water, so that it purified itself. Then the whole assembly killed it in the evening, struck the blood on the two side posts and the upper door post, and ate the flesh that night “roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs”.

“Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof.” It was eaten with the purtenance, for after those days there was nothing left within it.

Whatever the sacrifice is for the Lord, it has to be the best of the best, a flawless sacrifice, no bruise, no cut, no stain, nothing superfluous. The lamb that had no blemish was symbolic of Christ.

precepts.text: A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump; purge out the old leaven, for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.
precepts.point: That is why the Levitical laws of sacrifice are no longer performed: the law had a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image; those sacrifices offered year by year could never make the comers thereunto perfect, for it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. We needed Christ, the ultimate sacrifice. Read verse 1 again with that understanding: the offerings went up without blemish because they were symbolic of Christ's coming.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
“Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” A little sin in the spirit will get worse. “Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened.”

That is the true resemblance of the Passover: purging out sin not one day a year but constantly, in prayer and fasting. “For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us”. Christ is our Passover, our lamb without blemish, and the peace offering without blemish in Leviticus 3 points to him.

precepts.why:
Christ “loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word”. The sacrifice without blemish was given so the church could be made without blemish.

That is what the Levitical sacrifices figured.

precepts.text: The fat forbidden is the fat of the beast of which men offer an offering made by fire; it belongs to the laws of sacrifice.
precepts.point: Leviticus 7 answers it in context: whosoever eateth the fat of the beast of which men offer an offering made by fire unto the Lord shall be cut off. This is the law of sacrifice, which we are no longer under; Christ is the end of the law for righteousness. The sacrifices stopped after 70 AD at the fall of Jerusalem, when there was no longer a temple. And there is no way to take off all the fat of the meat you eat; we are not koshering our meat.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
Brothers and sisters ask whether we are cut off for eating fat. Having that question is a good thing; it means you are reading to understand, not reading just to say you read four chapters. Leviticus 7 answers it in context.

“Ye shall eat no manner of fat, of ox, or of sheep, or of goat. And the fat of the beast that dieth of itself, and the fat of that which is torn with beasts, may be used in any other use: but ye shall in no wise eat of it. For whosoever eateth the fat of the beast, of which men offer an offering made by fire unto the Lord, even the soul that eateth it shall be cut off from his people.”

The fat forbidden is the fat of the beast of which men offer an offering made by fire unto the Lord. This belongs to the law of sacrifice, which we are no longer under. And there is no way to take off all the fat of the meat you eat; we are not koshering our meat.

precepts.why:

The sacrifices stopped after 70 AD at the fall of Jerusalem, when there was no longer a temple. So the statute about the fat of the offering is not a statute we are cut off under today.

precepts.text: Ye shall eat no manner of blood; whatsoever soul eateth any manner of blood shall be cut off from his people.
precepts.point: The Lord put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel and sanctified his people with these laws; these laws make us special, going back to Deuteronomy 7 and 6, how he separated us. Do not follow the customs and fashions of the heathen.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
The blood is the other half of the perpetual statute, and it reads wider than the fat: “ye shall eat no manner of blood, whether it be of fowl or of beast, in any of your dwellings. Whatsoever soul it be that eateth any manner of blood, even that soul shall be cut off from his people.”

The blood was also for the altar of the Lord, but it is no manner of blood, of fowl or of beast, in any of your dwellings, and there is more to why the Lord had to say it: what Israel had learned in Egypt.

precepts.text: After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do; Israel had to be commanded away from what was learned there.
precepts.point: The Lord put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel and sanctified his people with these laws; these laws make us special, going back to Deuteronomy 7 and 6, how he separated us. Do not follow the customs and fashions of the heathen.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
After Israel came out of Egypt, we had learned heathen practices there, such as drinking blood. So the Lord said, “I am the Lord your God. After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do: neither shall ye walk in their ordinances.”

Drinking the blood of animals was an Egyptian custom tied to their idols, and the blood-drinking customs of the Hamitic nations continue to this day. Israel had to be commanded away from what was learned there; that is why the statute against eating blood had to be spoken.

precepts.text: The Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel; his laws sanctify his people.
precepts.point: The Lord put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel and sanctified his people with these laws; these laws make us special, going back to Deuteronomy 7 and 6, how he separated us. Do not follow the customs and fashions of the heathen.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
In Egypt the Lord said that “against any of the children of Israel shall not a dog move his tongue, against man or beast: that ye may know how that the Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel.”

The Lord put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel, and He sanctified His people with these laws. The statute not to eat blood, the Egyptian custom, is part of that difference: these laws make us special.

The dietary laws are part of that separation. It goes back to Deuteronomy 7 and 6, how He separated us: do not follow the customs and fashions of the heathen, and the blood they drink is one of them.

precepts.text: The people sinned against the Lord in eating with the blood; Saul had every man slay his beast on the great stone so they sinned not.
precepts.point: Serve the Lord and he shall bless thy bread and thy water, and take sickness away from the midst of thee: keep the dietary laws, what to eat and not eat, how to cook it and how to season it, and do not bow down to the gods of the heathen nor do after their works.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
Israel fell into this sin in Saul’s day. “Then they told Saul, saying, Behold, the people sin against the Lord, in that they eat with the blood. And he said, Ye have transgressed: roll a great stone unto me this day.” The people had flown upon the spoil and eaten with the blood, and Saul called it what it was: transgression.

Saul had every man bring his ox and his sheep and slay them on the great stone, “and sin not against the Lord in eating with the blood.” Eating with the blood is sin.

That is why you make sure your food is thoroughly cooked, well done, cut open to the bone so it cooks through. Meat served rare is not running with juice, it is blood.

precepts.text: Do not do after the works of the heathen; serve the Lord, and he shall bless thy bread and thy water and take sickness away from the midst of thee.

note.label: Leviticus 3: The Peace Offering Without Blemish

precepts.why:
The Lord brought Israel in unto the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, and said, “Thou shalt not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor do after their works”. Eating blood after the doings of Egypt is doing after the works of the heathen.

“And ye shall serve the Lord your God, and he shall bless thy bread, and thy water; and I will take sickness away from the midst of thee.” Keep the dietary laws, what to eat and not eat, how to cook it and how to season it, and do not bow down to the gods of the heathen nor do after their works; the blessing is on thy bread and thy water, and sickness taken away.
